o: We must transform each word of a space-separated sentence according to three simple rules: vowel-starting words get "ma" appended, consonant-starting words have their first letter moved to the end before "ma", and every word gets a suffix of 'a' characters equal to its 1-based index. For example, in "I speak Goat Latin": "I" starts with a vowel so it becomes "I" + "ma" + "a" = "Imaa"; "speak" becomes "peaks" + "ma" + "aa" = "peaksmaaa"; and so on. The constraints are tiny (length ≤ 150), so any straightforward simulation that processes each word once is more than fast enough. The only care needed is handling both cases of vowels ('a','e','i','o','u' and uppercase) and building the 'a'-suffix correctly per word index.
k: This is pure string simulation: split on spaces, transform each word independently, rejoin with spaces.
Vowel check must be case-insensitive since words may start with uppercase letters.
The number of trailing 'a's equals the word's 1-based index, so track an index counter while iterating.

a.n: Approach 1: Split, Transform Each Word, Rejoin
a.i: Split the sentence into words, apply the transformation rules to each word using its index, then join with single spaces. Since each word is processed in O(length) time and total length is bounded by 150, this linear scan is optimal. Building each result word with string concatenation or a list of parts keeps the code clean.
s: Split sentence into words by spaces.
Initialize an index counter starting at 1.
For each word: if its first character (lowercased) is a vowel, append "ma"; otherwise move the first character to the end and append "ma".
Append 'a' repeated `index` times, increment the index.
Join all transformed words with a single space and return.
a.t: O(n) where n is the total sentence length — every character is examined a constant number of times during splitting, transforming, and joining.
a.sp: O(n) for storing the split words and the output sentence.

a.i: Instead of splitting first, scan the sentence character by character, tracking the current word start. When a word ends (space or end of string), emit its transformed form immediately. This avoids materializing the intermediate word list, though asymptotically it is identical — useful mainly as a variant demonstrating streaming-style processing.
s: Iterate over indices; record where each word begins.
When hitting a space or end of string, extract the current word.
Apply the vowel/consonant rule plus "ma" and the index-suffix of 'a's.
Append the transformed word (with a separating space when needed) to the answer builder.
Return the built answer after the loop.
a.t: O(n) — one pass over the sentence with constant work per character.
a.sp: O(n) for the output builder (the input itself is not duplicated into a word list).

w: In an interview, go straight to Approach 1 — splitting and mapping is idiomatic, readable, and optimal at O(n); mention the streaming variant only if asked about avoiding intermediate allocations. Common pitfalls: forgetting case-insensitive vowel checks (e.g., "I" or "Goat"), miscounting the 'a' suffix (it is the 1-based word index, not 0-based), and accidentally producing leading/trailing spaces when joining manually. Edge cases include a single-word sentence and words that are entirely one letter. Likely follow-ups: handle punctuation attached to words, multiple/irregular whitespace, or process the sentence as a stream without random access.
